title: SPE Chapter 03 — Plugins
_comment: VET THIS FILE before rendering. Each scene = one short narration beat (aim 5-10s) + one visual. lane 'app' shows the running page at app-relative path (optional 'js' runs the app's Base API after load). lane 'code' shows a self-contained page built from the local source with lines hl highlighted. Rebuild: RESYNTH=1 bash scripts/make-episode.sh 03-Plugins

scenes.narr: Chapter three keeps the exact same look as before, but tears out the single class and replaces it with a real plugin architecture.
This is the whole idea in three lines: the request names a class and a method, and the code builds that plugin and calls that method.
Before any of that runs, a context object validates the three request parameters — which plugin, which method, which format — against strict allow-lists.
One small helper does the checking: read the parameter, test it against a pattern, and fall back to a safe default when it is missing or malformed.
Every plugin extends this abstract base, which defines the five basic actions — create, read, update, delete, and list — each defaulting to a friendly not-implemented stub.
A concrete plugin overrides only what it needs. Home implements just list, marked with the Override attribute so a typo can never silently create a new method.
Ask a plugin for a method it has not implemented, and the inherited stub answers honestly instead of crashing.
Ask for a plugin that does not exist, and the dispatcher returns a genuine 404 rather than a broken page.
The same request can answer in two formats: ask for JSON, and the very same data comes back as JSON instead of an HTML document.
So every page in the application is also an API endpoint, for free, with no extra code to write.
The Contact plugin shows a plugin reading shared state — the site's email address — straight from that one context object.
And there it is on the page: a working mailto link, built from that single shared value.
The entire program is still one expression — build the context, hand it to Init, and let it dispatch and render.
That is chapter three: the same three pages, now each a self-contained plugin. Next, chapter four splits every plugin cleanly into a model and a view.
